````bash
cd /home/mont9393/Documents/CSCI435/gitea
cat > .claude-students/README.md <<'EOF'
# .claude-students — start here

Course-only documentation for the CSCI-435 Gitea fork. It exists so a person — or an AI session —
can read one or two short pages instead of exploring ~150 Go packages. That exploration is the
single largest avoidable cost on this project, in your time and in tokens.

This page is the quick start: what is here, what tools you have, and the three things you will
actually need to do.

## Two layers, same content

| | `docs/` | `guide/` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Written for | an AI session | a person |
| Style | terse, every claim cites a file | explains, defines jargon, names symptoms |
| Length | ~80 lines | up to 200 |
| Status | **the source of truth** | a rendering of it |

Both have the same 34 filenames, so `guide/models-db.md` explains `docs/models-db.md`.

**`guide/` is derived from `docs/`.** Each guide stores a fingerprint of its source page, so if the
reference changes and the guide is not regenerated, the validator says so. **If the two ever
disagree, the guide is wrong** — fix the reference page, not the guide.

## What is in this folder

| File | What it is for |
| --- | --- |
| `INDEX.md` | Routing table: "working on X → read Y". Loaded into every AI session. |
| `guide/START-HERE.md` | **If you are new to this codebase, read this first.** |
| `guide/*.md` | A plain-English page per reference page. |
| `docs/*.md` | The reference pages. Terse, citation-heavy. |
| `MAINTENANCE.md` | The 22 rules. Read before editing anything here. |
| `_TEMPLATE.md`, `guide/_TEMPLATE.md` | The only permitted shapes for a new page. |
| `check.sh` | The validator. Run it before you push. |

## Your toolkit

One command:

```sh
./.claude-students/check.sh
```

It prints `check.sh: ok (34 docs, guide 34/34)` when everything is fine, or `file: message (rule N)`
for each problem. It is dependency-free and finishes in under a second.

It checks, among other things: that every page follows its template, stays under its line cap, cites
only paths that exist, and is listed in `INDEX.md`; that no two reference pages claim the same code;
that **every guide matches the fingerprint of its source page**; and that a guide cites no path its
source page does not — so a guide can add explanation, but never new facts.

## The three things you will actually do

### 1. You are new and want to understand the codebase

Read `guide/START-HERE.md`, then `guide/architecture.md`, then `guide/testing.md`. After that, read
only the page for whatever you are touching. Do not read all 34.

`INDEX.md` maps tasks to pages.

### 2. You found a page that is wrong or incomplete

This is expected, and fixing it is part of the work — not a favour.

1. Fix **`docs/<name>.md`**, never the guide. Every claim needs a repo path; no line numbers, only
   file plus symbol name.
2. Regenerate **`guide/<name>.md`** to match, and update its `source-hash` to the first 16
   characters of `sha256sum .claude-students/docs/<name>.md`.
3. Run `./.claude-students/check.sh`.
4. Ship both in the same pull request as the code change that taught you this, titled
   `docs(context): <subject>`.

If you skip step 2 the validator will tell you, by name, on the next run.

The easiest way to do step 2 is to ask an AI session: *"`docs/<name>.md` changed — regenerate
`guide/<name>.md` from it and update the hash."*

### 3. You are starting a fresh AI session

You do not have to do anything. `CLAUDE.md` imports `INDEX.md`, so every Claude session already has
the routing table, and `AGENTS.md` points other tools at it.

If a session starts exploring the tree instead of reading a page, say: *"Read
`.claude-students/INDEX.md` and use the page for this area."*

If you ask a session to change documentation here, point it at `MAINTENANCE.md` — rules 16-22 are
the ones about keeping the two layers in step.

## Not upstream

This folder is **ours**, not Gitea's, and is deliberately self-contained so it can be removed in one
step if this fork is ever merged upstream:

```sh
rm -rf .claude-students/
```

Then remove the two pointers: the `@.claude-students/INDEX.md` line in `CLAUDE.md`, and the
`.claude-students/INDEX.md` bullet in `AGENTS.md`. Nothing else refers to this folder — no
`Makefile` target, no CI job.

## Authority

These pages never override the project's own rules. `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and
`docs/guidelines-*.md` at the repository root are authoritative; the pages here summarise them and
point at code. If a page here contradicts one of those, the page here is wrong.

Note that `docs/` means two different things depending on where you are standing: inside this
folder it is our reference pages, at the repository root it is Gitea's own documentation. The guides
say "in this folder" or "Gitea's own" wherever it could be ambiguous.
EOF

Now there is. It didn't exist properly before you asked — here's what was missing and what I built.

## The gap that mattered most

`AGENTS.md` told every fresh session: *"Fix any doc you find wrong in the same PR."* After the guide layer landed, that instruction **causes a build failure**. An agent follows it, edits `docs/models-db.md`, and `check.sh` fails with a DRIFT error it was never told about. I created that trap when I added rule 18 and didn't update the pointer.

Fixed — the bullet now says editing a `docs/*.md` also requires regenerating its `guide/*.md` twin, and to run `check.sh` before pushing. Still one line; footprint still 2.

## `README.md` rewritten as the quick start

It predated the guide layer and never mentioned it. Now it covers:

- **Two layers, who reads which**, and that the guide is derived — so if they disagree, the guide is wrong.
- **Your toolkit**: the one command, what it prints, and what it actually enforces.
- **The three things you'll actually do:**
  1. *New and want to understand the codebase* → `START-HERE`, `architecture`, `testing`, then only your area.
  2. *Found a page that's wrong* → fix `docs/`, regenerate the guide, update the hash, run the validator, ship both in one PR. Including the practical shortcut: ask an AI session to regenerate it.
  3. *Starting a fresh AI session* → nothing to do, it's automatic; plus what to say if a session starts exploring instead of reading.
- Removal steps, and the `docs/` ambiguity (ours vs Gitea's).

## I tested the workflow I documented

Rather than assume it works, I ran it: appended a line to `docs/i18n.md` → validator named the file and said "regenerate it (rule 18)" → recomputed the hash exactly as the README instructs → `ok (34 docs, guide 34/34)`. The documented procedure is the procedure.

## And a small drift, caught immediately

The two front doors disagreed: `README.md` said reference pages are ~80 lines, `START-HERE.md` said ~90. Actual average is 80. Fixed — and it's a fair illustration of why the hash mechanism exists, since prose that *sounds* right drifts silently while a fingerprint cannot.

`START-HERE.md` now also points at `README.md` for the toolkit, so the human path is: START-HERE (understand the code) → README (maintain the docs) → MAINTENANCE (the rules behind it).

## Final state

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `check.sh` | ok (34 docs, guide 34/34) |
| markdownlint, all 75 files | clean |
| Footprint outside the folder | 2 insertions |
| Removal rehearsal | returns to HEAD |

One thing I'd flag: I can verify the instructions are *accurate*, but not that they're *clear to someone who isn't me*. The real test is handing `README.md` §2 to a teammate who hasn't seen any of this and asking them to fix a doc. Whatever they have to ask about is the gap.

```text
=== conventional commit types allowed ===
In the PR summary, you can describe exactly how you are fixing this problem.

PR titles must follow the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) format, because PRs are squash-merged and the PR title becomes the resulting commit message:

```text
type(scope)!: subject
```

The scope in parentheses is optional. A `!` immediately before the colon marks a [breaking change](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/#summary): either `type!:` or `type(scope)!:` (not `type!(scope):`).

Use one of these types:

- `build`: Changes affecting the build system, packaging, or external dependencies
- `ci`: Changes to CI/CD configuration files and scripts
- `chore`: Maintenance changes that do not affect production code or should not appear in the changelog
- `docs`: Documentation-only changes
- `feat`: A larger user-facing feature, improvement, or new functionality
- `enhance`: Small or trivial user-facing improvements or UX polish (for example wording changes, color adjustments, spacing or padding tweaks, placeholders, small UI behavior improvements)
- `fix`: A bug fix, UX correction, or security-related dependency update
- `perf`: Performance improvements (speed, memory, scalability)
- `refactor`: A code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature
- `revert`: Reverts a previous change
- `style`: Formatting or style-only changes that do not affect code behavior (for example lint-driven edits)
- `test`: Adding or correcting tests
```
</details></tool-use>

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-11 02:28:03Z)**_

Diagnosed. Nothing is wrong with the commit or the branch — it's a GitHub permissions problem.

## What's actually happening

```
remote: Permission to CSCI-435-SE/gitea.git denied to amanb-os.
403
```

| Fact | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Git authenticates as GitHub user **`amanb-os`** | the 403 message names it |
| The cached credential is an OAuth token, not a password | stored username is `287293730`, a numeric ID — typical of VS Code / GitHub CLI auth via libsecret |
| Read works | `git ls-remote` and `git fetch` both succeed |
| …but that proves nothing | the repo is **public** (unauthenticated API returns 200), so anyone can read it |
| Write is denied | the 403 |

So `amanb-os` can see the repo like any stranger, and has no push rights.

## Most likely causes, in order

**1. `amanb-os` was never added as a collaborator** — or an invite is sitting unaccepted. STUDENTS.md claims "all team members have write access", so this is the likely gap. Check <https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/invitations> and your GitHub notifications; if there's nothing, ask whoever owns the repo to add `amanb-os`.

**2. The cached token belongs to the wrong account.** Your git identity is `abhoot <abhoot@wm.edu>` but GitHub sees `amanb-os`. If your course account is a different handle, the stored credential is the wrong one. Clear it with:

```sh
printf 'protocol=https\nhost=github.com\n' | git credential reject
```

The next push will re-prompt.

**3. The token lacks write scope** — a fine-grained PAT without Contents: write, for instance. Re-authenticating fixes this too.

## A note on your setup

You have no `gh` CLI installed, which is why I couldn't query your permissions directly. `gh` would make this a one-liner (`gh auth status`, `gh repo view --json viewerPermission`) and is generally worth having for this course.

Your work is safe either way — commit `301fecc005` is on `chore/claude-students-docs` locally, nothing is lost, and the push will just work once access is sorted. I haven't touched your credentials or the remote; those are yours to change.

That's the answer: **VS Code is supplying the credential**, not the keyring.

```
GIT_ASKPASS = /usr/share/code/resources/app/extensions/git/dist/askpass.sh
TERM_PROGRAM = vscode
```

You're signed into VS Code as `amanb-os`, and its Git extension hands that token to every push. Clearing the system keyring wouldn't help — VS Code would just re-inject the same account.

## Fix it in VS Code

1. Click the **account icon** (bottom-left of the sidebar, above the gear).
2. You'll see something like *"amanb-os (GitHub)"* — click it → **Sign Out**.
3. Sign back in with the account that has access to `CSCI-435-SE/gitea`.
4. Push again. VS Code will prompt and authorise with the new account.

If the old account lingers, also clear the stored credential:

```
! printf 'protocol=https\nhost=github.com\n' | git credential reject
```

(The `!` prefix runs it here so I can see the result.)

## If you'd rather not depend on VS Code at all

Two options that sidestep this entirely:

**SSH** — no tokens, no editor involvement:
```sh
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:CSCI-435-SE/gitea.git
```
(assuming you have an SSH key on the right account)

**`gh` CLI** — also gives you the permission-checking commands I couldn't run earlier:
```sh
sudo zypper install gh   # openSUSE, based on your system
gh auth login
gh auth setup-git
```

## Worth confirming either way

`amanb-os` being the wrong account is one explanation for the 403 — but it's worth checking that your *correct* account actually has write access before you conclude that's the whole story. Once signed in as the right user, `git ls-remote` will still work (the repo is public), so the real test is the push itself. If it still 403s, you're not a collaborator yet and someone needs to add you.

Your commit is untouched on `chore/claude-students-docs` regardless.
